Sublinear operator

Words: 370 Articles: 6
Functional analysis OurBigBook.com
A nonnegative function-valued operator S is sublinear if S(f+g)≤S(f)+S(g) and S(cf)=∣c∣S(f) almost everywhere. This pointwise domination notion includes maximal one-sided interval averaging operators and differs from requiring an ordinary linear map.

Weak-type operator (μ{∣Sf∣>λ}≤(C∥f∥p​/λ)q)

Words: 344 Articles: 5
Sublinear operator OurBigBook.com
An operator has weak type (p,q), with finite q, if the displayed bound holds for every input and every λ>0, with one constant independent of both. It controls the distribution of its output rather than requiring its strong Lq norm to be finite.

Strong Lp bound from weak L1 and L-infinity bounds (∥Sf∥pp​≤2pqC1​C∞p−1​∥f∥pp​)

Words: 67
Weak-type operator OurBigBook.com
Let S be a sublinear operator with positive constants and μ{Sf>a}≤C1​∥f∥1​/a and ∥Sf∥∞​≤C∞​∥f∥∞​. Split f into its part above a/(2C∞​) and its bounded remainder. The latter contributes at most a/2, so the weak bound controls the superlevel measure by 2C1​a−1∫∣f∣>a/(2C∞​)​∣f∣. Integrating this estimate with layer cake representation proves the displayed bound for 1<p<∞ and q=p/(p−1). In particular it gives the strong Lp estimate for the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function.

Weak type with a normed domain (λ{∣Tf∣>a}≤(C∥f∥E​/a)q)

Words: 122 Articles: 1
Weak-type operator OurBigBook.com
For a normed space E and 0<q<∞, an operator T:E→L0 is of weak type (E,q) when the displayed distribution bound holds uniformly over f∈E and a>0. No completeness of E is needed. A sublinear operator has pointwise triangle domination and absolute homogeneity; its outputs may be understood modulo almost everywhere equality.
Dense approximation under a weak-type maximal bound
Words: 73
Weak type with a normed domain OurBigBook.com
Suppose linear operators At​ and A0​ on a normed space satisfy ∣At​f∣,∣A0​f∣≤Sf, where S has weak type with a normed domain, and all relevant suprema are measurable. If At​g→A0​g almost everywhere on a dense subspace, the same holds for every input. For a fixed approximation g, the limiting error is at most 2S(f−g). The measure where it exceeds a is at most (2C∥f−g∥/a)q, which tends to zero as the approximation improves. This is a convergence-to-a-specified-limit version of almost-everywhere convergence from weak-type domination.

Weak type (1,1) (μ{Sf>λ}≤C∥f∥1​/λ)

Words: 110 Articles: 1
Weak-type operator OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative sublinear operator, weak type (1,1) is the displayed level-set bound for all integrable inputs and positive thresholds. It supplies an exceptional-set estimate for approximation errors; the uncentered maximal weak-type inequality is a central example.
Almost-everywhere convergence from weak-type domination
Words: 78
Weak type (1,1) OurBigBook.com
Suppose a family of linear operators, including its limiting operator, is pointwise dominated by a sublinear operator of weak type (1,1). Convergence almost everywhere on an L1-dense subspace then extends to every L1 input. Approximate the input by errors of norm at most 2−2n. The weak estimate and the Borel-Cantelli first lemma make the corresponding domination errors tend to zero almost everywhere. Linearity bounds the difference between the full and approximating convergence errors by twice that domination error. This argument does not need an uncountable supremum to be measurable.

Operator algebra

Words: 557 Articles: 11
Functional analysis OurBigBook.com
An operator algebra is an algebra of linear operators, with multiplication given by composition. In quantum examples it can be generated by creation and annihilation operators subject to the canonical commutation relations or canonical anticommutation relations. Its analytic realization requires specifying a common domain for unbounded operators.

Quasi-local observable algebra (A=⋃Λ​AΛ​​∥⋅∥)

Words: 74
Operator algebra OurBigBook.com
For a lattice system, finite-region observable algebras AΛ​ embed into larger ones by tensoring with the identity. Their union has a norm closure called the quasi-local observable algebra, a C-star algebra. It describes finite-support observables and norm limits of such observables. An operator flipping every spin of an infinite lattice need not belong to it: successive finite-region flips are not norm-Cauchy. Restrictions to this algebra can therefore lose relative-phase information retained by increasingly nonlocal finite-system observables.

Cyclic vector for an operator algebra (AΩ=H)

Words: 207 Articles: 4
Operator algebra OurBigBook.com
A vector is cyclic for an operator algebra when its orbit under that algebra has dense linear span. This is distinct from requiring the powers of one chosen operator to span the space. If the algebra is linear, its orbit itself is already a vector subspace.

Separating vector for an operator algebra (aΩ=0⟹a=0)

Words: 165 Articles: 3
Cyclic vector for an operator algebra OurBigBook.com
A vector is separating for an operator algebra when evaluation at that vector is injective. A cyclic vector for the commutant of an operator algebra is separating for the original algebra: if aΩ=0, then a vanishes on its dense commutant orbit.
Tomita operator (S0​(aΩ)=a∗Ω)
Words: 133 Articles: 2
Separating vector for an operator algebra OurBigBook.com
For a Von Neumann algebra with a cyclic separating vector, this is a densely defined antilinear operator. It is closable: the commutant orbit lies in the domain of its antilinear adjoint and is dense. Write S for its closure and S=JΔ1/2 for its polar decomposition. In finite dimension it is everywhere defined and invertible. For a tracial vector, S0​ is isometric and extends to an antiunitary involution.
Modular operator (Δ=S∗S)
Words: 29
Tomita operator OurBigBook.com
The positive operator in the polar decomposition S=JΔ1/2 of the Tomita operator. In a matrix-algebra standard representation with cyclic vector D>0, it is Δ(X)=D2XD−2. For a tracial vector it is the identity.
Modular conjugation (J)

A Von Neumann algebra whose center consists exactly of scalar multiples of the identity. A group von Neumann algebra is a factor exactly when every nonidentity conjugacy class is infinite. Conversely, the sum of left translations over a finite nonidentity class is a nonscalar central operator.

Skorokhod space (D([0,1],R))

Words: 83
Function space OurBigBook.com
The Skorokhod space consists of real paths that are right-continuous and have a finite left limit at every positive time. Its J1​ topology allows small changes of time: xn​→x when there are increasing homeomorphisms λn​ of [0,1] such that ∥λn​−id∥∞​→0 and ∥xn​∘λn​−x∥∞​→0, where id denotes the identity time map. This topology aligns nearby jumps rather than insisting on uniform closeness at identical times. The step-path version of the Donsker invariance principle converges here to continuous Brownian motion; its polygonal version uses the ordinary supremum norm on continuous paths.

A normed vector space is a vector space equipped with a norm, whose induced metric is d(x,y)=∥x−y∥.

Interior and closure of norm balls (intB(0,1)=B(0,1),B(0,1)​=B(0,1))

Words: 76
Normed vector space OurBigBook.com
In a nonzero normed vector space, a unit vector x is approached from outside the unit ball by (1+ε)x, so no boundary point is interior. It is approached from inside by (1−ε)x, so every boundary point is in the closure of the open ball. The zero space satisfies the same identities trivially. These statements need the radial structure of a normed space; a two-point discrete metric space with interpoint distance one disproves both analogous claims for general metric balls.

Strictly convex normed space geometry gives ∥f−(u+v)/2∥<d, a contradiction. If d=0, both elements equal f. This proves uniqueness when a best approximant exists, without asserting existence for a nonclosed subspace.

Given f in a normed vector space and a vector subspace U, an element p∗​∈U is a best approximation if ∥f−p∗​∥=infp∈U​∥f−p∥. Existence is automatic for a finite-dimensional vector subspace: a minimizing sequence can be bounded by the triangle inequality, and a subsequence converges by compactness in finite dimension. An arbitrary infinite-dimensional vector subspace need not contain a minimizer. The norm matters: best uniform approximation uses the supremum norm, while L1 approximation minimizes integrated absolute error.

The convex hull of a finite union of compact convex sets is compact: group the terms by their set and use the simplex parametrization. The point must lie in that hull, contrary to extremality. The closures are in the given Hausdorff locally convex topology.

Lax-Milgram theorem

Words: 453 Articles: 7
Functional analysis OurBigBook.com
The theorem supplies solvability for a coercive weak formulation.
A bounded bilinear form a on a real Hilbert space H that is a coercive bilinear form represents every bounded linear functional uniquely: for each ℓ∈H′, there is a unique u∈H with a(u,v)=ℓ(v) for every v∈H.
For a proof, the Riesz representation theorem gives a bounded linear operator T and a vector g with a(u,v)=⟨Tu,v⟩ and ℓ(v)=⟨g,v⟩. Coercivity and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality give ∥Tu∥≥α∥u∥, so T is injective and its image is closed: convergence of Tun​ makes un​ a Cauchy sequence, whose limit supplies the image limit. If v belongs to the orthogonal complement of the image, then a(u,v)=0 for every u; setting u=v and using coercivity forces v=0. Thus the image is also dense and equals H. There is consequently a unique u with Tu=g, and ∥u∥≤∥ℓ∥/α. The complex version uses a bounded sesquilinear form with Rea(u,u)≥α∥u∥2.

Choose aU​ in each bounded component of C∖K. Every nonvanishing continuous function on K extends nonvanishingly to a neighborhood. Use finite-hole neighborhoods of a planar compact set within that neighborhood, and subtract its finite list of winding obstructions by multiplying by ∏(z−aU​)−kU​. The continuous logarithm lifting criterion gives the remaining exponential. Uniqueness follows by extending a purported logarithm of such a finite product to a smaller neighborhood: a small multiplicative error has a local logarithm, whereas its winding around the Uth hole is kU​. Thus all kU​ vanish. The quotient by exponentials is the free abelian group on the bounded complementary components; each element has finite support.

This does not contradict preservation of ordinary convergence, since the constructed sequence is divergent.

For a strongly continuous semigroup, apply the bounded operator Tt​ to the difference quotient defining its semigroup generator. The limit proves domain invariance and commutation on the generator domain. This is not an assertion that the unbounded generator acts on every vector.

Generator of a strongly continuous semigroup is closed and densely defined

Words: 61
Infinitesimal generator of a semigroup OurBigBook.com
The Yosida averaging of a semigroup gives xh​=h−1∫0h​S(t)xdt∈D(A) with xh​→x, proving that the generator domain is dense. For x∈D(A), the Bochner integral identity S(t)x−x=∫0t​S(s)Axds holds. If xn​→x and Axn​→y, pass to the limit in this identity and divide by t. The strongly continuous semigroup property makes the resulting limit y, so x∈D(A) and Ax=y. This proves that the infinitesimal generator of a semigroup is a closed operator.

The generator domain consists of the vectors whose semigroup orbit is right-differentiable at zero. It is a dense linear subspace, and the generator is closed.

Equip D(A) with its graph norm. The restrictions U(t)∣D(A)​ form a C0-semigroup on this Banach space; its generator is A restricted to D(A2).

(zI−A)−1x=∫0∞​e−ztU(t)xdt.

On a Hilbert space, an operator A is dissipative when Re(Ax,x)≤0 for every x∈D(A). This is the infinitesimal form of norm contraction.

Positive spectrum of a dissipative operator is adjoint point spectrum (α∈σ(Z)⟺α∈σp​(Z∗)(α>0))

Words: 58
Dissipative operator OurBigBook.com
For a closed densely defined dissipative operator, the estimate ∥(αI−Z)f∥≥α∥f∥ makes its range closed and its kernel trivial. Thus a positive spectral value means this range is proper, which is equivalent to a nonzero vector in ker(αI−Z∗). Dissipativity is essential: a real multiplication operator may have positive continuous spectrum with no adjoint eigenvector.

Dissipative Cayley-transform contraction (∥(I−hL/2)−1(I+hL/2)∥2​≤1)

Words: 57
Dissipative operator OurBigBook.com
If Re⟨Lv,v⟩≤0 in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, I−hL/2 is invertible for every positive h. The relation v+​−v−​=(h/2)L(v+​+v−​) gives ∥v+​∥2−∥v−​∥2=(h/2)Re⟨L(v+​+v−​),v+​+v−​⟩≤0. Thus the Crank-Nicolson method contracts for such a linear system even when L is a non-normal matrix. This is a direct energy result, not an unqualified inequality by a scalar rational function evaluated at a logarithmic norm.

A maximal dissipative operator is dissipative and has no proper dissipative extension. Equivalently, for a densely defined dissipative operator, λI−A is onto for some positive λ.

The Lumer-Phillips theorem says that a densely defined operator generates a contraction C0-semigroup exactly when it is maximal dissipative.

Strongly continuous unitary group

Words: 216 Articles: 4
C0-semigroup OurBigBook.com
A strongly continuous unitary group is a family U(t) for all real t that is strongly continuous, obeys the group law, and preserves the Hilbert norm. Its generator is skew-adjoint; conversely, every skew-adjoint operator generates such a group.

Stone's theorem on one-parameter unitary groups (Ut​=eitA,A=A∗)

Words: 55
Strongly continuous unitary group OurBigBook.com
Every strongly continuous unitary group has a unique possibly unbounded self-adjoint operator A as its generator. Its domain consists of the vectors for which the norm limit of (Ut​ξ−ξ)/(it) exists as t→0. Conversely, the Borel functional calculus for a normal operator constructs a strongly continuous unitary group from every self-adjoint A. Smooth averaging supplies a dense generator domain; Laplace integrals of Ut​ and U−t​ prove that A±i are surjective, which establishes self-adjointness.

Skew-adjoint generator

Words: 123 Articles: 2
Strongly continuous unitary group OurBigBook.com
An operator A is skew-adjoint when A∗=−A. Both A and −A are then maximal dissipative, and the generated group is unitary.
Even rank of a skew-adjoint linear map (rankA∈2N0​)
Words: 61
Skew-adjoint generator OurBigBook.com
On a finite-dimensional real inner product space, a skew-adjoint operator has even rank. In an orthonormal basis its matrix is skew-symmetric, so an invertible such matrix must have even dimension by detA=det(−A)=(−1)ddetA. Moreover kerA=(imA)⊥, so the image and kernel intersect trivially. The restriction of A to its image is an invertible skew-adjoint map, and its dimension, the rank, is therefore even.
Skew-adjoint nilpotent operators vanish (A∗=−A, Ak=0 ⟹ A=0)
Words: 40
Skew-adjoint generator OurBigBook.com
On a finite-dimensional positive inner-product space, a skew-adjoint nilpotent operator is zero. In an orthonormal basis, ∥A∥F2​=tr(A∗A)=−tr(A2)=0, since a nilpotent matrix has zero trace and so does its square. The Frobenius norm therefore vanishes. In particular, a nonzero nilpotent adjoint map rules out a compact Lie algebra.

Abstract Cauchy problem

Words: 319 Articles: 9
C0-semigroup OurBigBook.com
An abstract Cauchy problem has the form Z′(t)=AZ(t)+F(t) in a Banach space, where A may be unbounded and generates the homogeneous evolution.

Classical solution of an abstract Cauchy problem (u′=Lu+f)

Words: 85
Abstract Cauchy problem OurBigBook.com
For a closed operator L on a Banach space H, a positive-time classical solution belongs to C([0,T],H)∩C1((0,T],H), takes values in D(L) for positive time, and has Lu∈C((0,T],H). It satisfies the differential equation and the initial condition in H. Classical regularity also at time zero requires the corresponding regularity of the initial datum, in particular u0​∈D(L). For an analytic semigroup and Hölder continuous forcing, the variation-of-constants formula gives such a solution: subtracting the forcing at the current time turns the singular estimate ∥LS(r)∥≤C/r into the integrable bound Crθ−1.

Words: 85 Articles: 2
Abstract Cauchy problem OurBigBook.com
A nonautonomous abstract Cauchy problem has the form u′(t)=A(t)u(t), with a time-dependent generally closed linear operator. Under stability, common-domain, and regularity hypotheses, it is propagated by an evolution family.

An evolution family consists of bounded operators U(t,s) for s≤t satisfying U(s,s)=I and U(t,r)U(r,s)=U(t,s). For sufficiently regular data it solves ∂t​U(t,s)x=A(t)U(t,s)x and ∂s​U(t,s)x=−U(t,s)A(s)x.

For a partition s=t0​<⋯<tN​=t, the frozen-generator approximation is
UN​(t,s)=e(tN​−tN−1​)A(tN−1​)⋯e(t1​−t0​)A(t0​).
(61)
Under the hypotheses of the nonautonomous generation theorem, these products converge strongly and uniformly on compact time triangles to the evolution family.

Z(t)=U(t)Z0​+∫0t​U(t−s)F(s)ds.

A semilinear abstract Cauchy problem has Z′=AZ+N(Z), where the linear part generates a C0-semigroup and the nonlinear map is typically locally Lipschitz on the phase space.

A local mild solution is a fixed point of the nonlinear variation-of-constants map in C([0,T];X). Local Lipschitz continuity of the nonlinearity gives existence and uniqueness for sufficiently small T.

For a locally Lipschitz semilinear evolution, a maximal mild solution either exists for all positive time or its phase-space norm becomes unbounded as the finite maximal time is approached.
